DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders Evaluation, 2025-26

**Overall:** The report does not support its headline causal claim or its recommendation as written. It also contains an arithmetic error that undermines the author's "success" framing.

## 1. The overall uptake figure is wrong
Table 1's own numbers give 13,772 / 22,080 = **62.4%**, not 66.0%. That is below the 65% national ambition, so the claim that Eastvale exceeded it "for the first time" is false. The author repeats this as "good news", and the report states it in Section 3. The error needs correcting before the report goes anywhere. The group rows check out (70.0% and 57.0%, consent 75% and ~61.5%, and 93.3% and 92.7% of consented children vaccinated). The 66% total also doesn't match any simple average of the two groups.

## 2. The 13-point gap is not evidence that reminders caused the difference
Schools opted in, and the report itself shows the opt-in group differed systematically:
- 29 of 38 reminder schools have a full-time school nurse, against 11 of 54 others.
- Reminder schools skew towards the more affluent west.
- Non-reminder schools skew towards eastern wards with more households that speak another language at home, higher mobility, and incomplete paper forms.

Nurse presence, affluence and engagement plausibly raise uptake on their own. Opting in is also a marker of a better-organised school. There is no pre-period baseline (2024-25 uptake by school), so no difference-in-differences is possible. Statements such as "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 points" and "the clearest evidence we have" are unjustified. The true effect could be much smaller, or even close to zero. The author's "clean side-by-side comparison" is not clean.

## 3. The effect is unlikely to transfer to the schools that would receive it
- In non-reminder schools only **61%** of families have a valid mobile number, against 93% in reminder schools. Reminders cannot reach about 4 in 10 families there. The 93% coverage may itself be a reason schools could opt in successfully.
- The reminder links to the online portal. The groups driving low uptake (language barriers, paper forms returned incomplete, high mobility) may be the least responsive to this channel.
- Uptake in non-reminder schools ranges from 38% to 79%. A single average effect applied to all of them ignores that heterogeneity.

So "57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" is an extrapolation with no support. The £2,500 set-up charge and the cost of fixing contact data are also unlikely to cover a 39% gap in numbers.

## 4. The cost analysis is less "cautious" than claimed
- It assumes all three messages go to all non-consenting families, but it ignores that many have no valid number. Costs may be overstated, and benefits overstated by more.
- It counts "families" but uses child counts (4,990 non-consenting pupils). Siblings make these differ.
- It leaves out staff time, data cleaning, and the cost of non-text follow-up. The arithmetic itself is fine (~£1,200 + £550 + £2,500 ≈ £4,250).
- Cost per additional child vaccinated is never calculated, and it is the figure that matters.

## 5. Unsupported comparative claims
"More than any other intervention we have tried" and "by far the cheapest route" are never backed by data. The only comparator is mop-up sessions (+3–6 points), which were run in just 14 schools. Where those schools were, and whether they overlap with reminder schools, is not reported. Mop-up may be more effective in the eastern wards, where reminders reach fewer people.

## 6. Reasoning and process concerns
- "Consent is the bottleneck" is reasonable, since 92–93% of consented children were vaccinated in both groups. But it doesn't show that text reminders are the right lever for consent, particularly for the unreached groups in Section 4.
- The author says they "looked hard for reasons not to scale" and found none, yet the report contains several (confounding, contact coverage, language, nurse presence). That suggests confirmation bias.
- Rolling out to all 92 schools at once removes any future comparison group. A staggered or randomised rollout, for example starting with non-reminder schools stratified by nurse presence and phone coverage, would give real evidence for little extra cost.

## Suggested fixes
1. Correct the overall uptake to 62.4%, and remove the "above national ambition" claim.
2. Reframe the 13 points as an unadjusted association. Add 2024-25 school-level baselines and adjust for nurse presence, deprivation and phone coverage.
3. Report the effect within comparable subgroups, such as nurse and non-nurse schools, east and west.
4. Add a plan for improving contact data and offering non-text routes (translated materials, simpler consent forms, targeted mop-ups) for the unreached families.
5. Compare the cost per additional vaccinated child for reminders and for mop-ups.
6. Recommend a phased, evaluated rollout rather than immediate universal adoption, with realistic expected gains in place of "around 70%".
